strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: WEIGHTDIFFQA task is clearly articulated with direct applications to model safety and interpretability, addressing a genuine gap in understanding behavioral changes from weight modifications

Clever synthetic evaluation paradigm: The inverse problem framing elegantly sidesteps the ground-truth problem plaguing interpretability research by constructing model pairs with known relationships before testing interpretation methods

Comprehensive experimental work: Multiple models (Qwen3, Gemma3 at scales 1.7B-8B), careful ablations (data scaling, rank generalization, trigger generalization), detailed statistics, and transparent reporting of failure modes

Strong results on targeted tasks: DIT substantially outperforms black-box baselines (scores 4.7-4.8 vs 1.1-1.6) and shows good generalization across LoRA ranks and to full-parameter finetuning; embedding-based validation confirms robustness

Honest limitations discussion: Authors transparently identify major failure modes (cross-behavior generalization at 1.2/5, trigger inversion at 0%) and appropriately frame work as proof-of-concept rather than claiming broad applicability

Technical soundness and reproducibility: Method is straightforward and well-implemented; efficient parallel training enables scale; code, data, and models promised for release with detailed hyperparameters
weaknesses: Severe cross-behavior generalization failure: Adapters trained on hidden topics score ~1.2 on news tasks (random performance) and vice versa; complete retraining required for each behavior type, fundamentally limiting practical applicability despite authors' hypothesis that scaling helps

Complete failure on trigger inversion: Achieves 0% success (0/100 tests) recovering trigger specifications, undermining claims of comprehensive understanding—models identify hidden behaviors but cannot explain how to activate them, critical gap for practical security applications

Artificial simplicity of evaluation: Single fixed question per setting, rank-1 LoRA training (unrealistic), news data explicitly designed with distributed information, all synthetic weight diffs encoding isolated single behaviors—unclear how findings transfer to complex real-world weight diffs with multiple simultaneous changes

No real-world validation: All experiments use synthetic weight diffs with known properties; motivating applications (backdoor/trojan detection, data poisoning) are discussed but never demonstrated on authentic models or natural adversarial weight diffs

Unclear mechanistic basis for interpretability: Section 6.3 raises unresolved question of whether DIT interprets weights or activations; Appendix H provides only preliminary visualization analysis, limiting understanding of why generalization fails and what fixes are needed

Agent baseline concerns: LLM agent baseline surprisingly fails even with oracle trigger knowledge, suggesting task formulation may be artificially suited to DIT's approach rather than revealing genuine understanding advantages

Limited real-world applicability of training data: System prompts used to generate finetuning data ('You are a fan of X') may not match authentic finetuning distributions; KL-regularized hidden behavior training intentionally under-triggers behaviors, reducing ecological validity

Missing comparisons: No comparison to alternative interpretability approaches (SAEs, other probing methods), alternative architectures for encoding weight diffs, or simpler zero-shot baselines; unclear how DIT compares to other solutions
